title: Evaluate, Validate, and Report Assessment Findings
intro: Turning test results into decisions: triaging findings by severity, exploitability, reproducibility and business impact; telling security vulnerabilities apart from model limitations such as hallucinations; mapping findings to MITRE ATLAS, the OWASP Top 10s and CWE; documenting evidence so findings can be reproduced and retested; and communicating risk clearly to technical and non-technical audiences.
objectives: Triage AI assessment findings using severity, exploitability, reproducibility, business impact, reach and detectability
Distinguish security vulnerabilities from model limitations and safety issues, and route each to the right owner
Correlate findings with industry frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS, the OWASP Top 10s and CWE
Document evidence and reproduction packages that hold up despite non-determinism, while protecting sensitive material
Communicate AI risk to engineers, leaders, legal teams and vendors in the form each needs

scenes.title: Which findings matter most?
scenes.sub: Triage by severity, exploitability, reproducibility and impact
scenes.say: A good assessment produces dozens of findings, and they are not equal. Some need fixing before launch; others belong on a backlog. Triage decides which is which, quickly and consistently. | This video covers how to triage AI assessment findings by severity, exploitability, reproducibility and business impact.

scenes.title: Six triage factors

items.d: One user, one tenant or everyone

scenes.say: Six factors drive AI triage. | Severity: the worst credible consequence, such as data exfiltration or an unauthorised payment. | Exploitability: how much skill, access and effort an attacker needs. Can an anonymous user do it, or only an insider? | Reproducibility: how often it works. For AI, that is a success rate across repeated attempts, not a yes or a no. | Business impact: the effect on customers, money, legal obligations and reputation. | Reach: whether it affects one user, one tenant, or every user. | And detectability: whether monitoring would notice it happening.

scenes.title: From raw finding to tracked fix
scenes.say: Triage turns raw findings into tracked fixes in six steps. First, validate: reproduce the finding, and rule out test errors, such as a misconfigured staging environment or an over-generous automated judge. | Deduplicate: many variants often share one root cause, so group them into one finding, with the variants kept as evidence. | Rate the finding’s severity, exploitability and success rate. | Prioritise, by weighing business impact and reach against your risk appetite. | Assign an owner, a deadline linked to the priority, and an interim control if the fix will take time. | And track the finding to closure: fix it, retest it, and close it only when the retest passes.

scenes.code:

severity: high (unauthorised refunds)
exploitability: any customer; one email needed
reproducibility: 31 of 100 attempts (31%)
business impact: direct loss; regulator interest
reach: every customer mailbox the agent reads
detected: no alert raised during testing

owner: payments agent team; retest by 21 Nov

notes.d: Consistent, traceable decisions.
The finding and its worst credible consequence.
Anyone can try; it works almost a third of the time.
Direct loss, regulatory interest, every mailbox.
Silence raises the priority.
Priority, owner and a retest date.

scenes.say: Here is a triage record for one finding. Every finding gets one, so decisions are consistent and traceable. | Finding F-07: an instruction hidden in a customer email can make the support agent call its refund tool. Severity is high, because the result is an unauthorised refund. | It is easy to exploit, because any customer can send an email. And it is reproducible: it worked in thirty-one of a hundred attempts. | The business impact is direct financial loss and regulatory interest, and it reaches every mailbox the agent reads. | No alert fired during testing, which raises the priority further. | So it is priority one: fix before launch, with a named owner and a retest date.

scenes.say: To recap. | Weigh severity, exploitability, reproducibility, business impact, reach and detectability. | Validate and deduplicate findings before rating them. | Use a documented rubric, and record the reasoning behind each priority. | And assign owners and deadlines, closing findings only after a passing retest.

blocks.md:
### Triage factors for AI findings
| Factor | Question | AI-specific notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Severity** | What is the worst credible consequence? | Agency raises severity: a finding that triggers actions or reaches data outranks one that only produces text |
| **Exploitability** | Who can do it, with what access, skill and effort? | Natural-language attacks need little skill, and indirect injection needs no access to the system at all |
| **Reproducibility** | How often does it work? | Report a success rate over many attempts, with settings; even 5% is frequent at scale (Module 6.4) |
| **Business impact** | What does it cost customers and the organisation? | Include regulatory exposure, such as personal data or a high-risk system under the EU AI Act |
| **Reach** | One user, one tenant or everyone? | Shared memory, indexes or caches can spread one injection to many users |
| **Detectability** | Would monitoring notice? | Undetected attacks raise priority (Module 5.3) |

### Scoring and priority
Generic scores such as **CVSS** capture some of this, but miss AI-specific factors such as non-determinism and agency. Use them as inputs, alongside emerging AI scoring such as **OWASP AIVSS** (Module 5.4), and a documented internal rubric that maps factors to priorities:
| Priority | Typical profile | Response |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | Severe impact, easy to exploit, reproducible | Fix or block before launch; interim controls now |
| **P2** | Severe but hard to exploit, or moderate and easy | Fix within a set period; monitor for attempts |
| **P3** | Limited impact | Planned backlog, or accept with sign-off if justified |

### The triage workflow
1. **Validate** each finding: reproduce it, and rule out test artefacts such as a staging misconfiguration or a lenient automated judge.
2. **Deduplicate** variants that share a root cause.
3. **Rate and prioritise** using the rubric, and record the reasoning.
4. **Assign** an owner, a deadline linked to the priority and, where needed, an interim control such as disabling a tool (Module 6.6).
5. **Track** each finding to closure, closing it only after a passing retest. Accepted risks go to the risk register with an owner and a review date (Module 2.3).

blocks.title: Two findings, one slot
blocks.md: A team has time to fix one finding before launch. **Finding A:** a jailbreak makes the public chatbot write rude jokes, in 40% of attempts. **Finding B:** an instruction hidden in uploaded documents makes the agent email file contents to an external address, in 3% of attempts.

q.q: Which finding should be fixed FIRST?
o: Finding A, because its 40% success rate makes it far more reproducible than B
Finding B, because data exfiltration from uploaded files is far more severe
Neither, because both findings succeed in fewer than half of all attempts
Finding A, because reputational harm always outweighs data protection issues
q.why: Severity and business impact dominate. Emailing file contents to an outsider is a serious security and privacy breach, and 3% is frequent at scale. Rude jokes are a content issue to fix, but at a lower priority.

blocks.title: Triage questions
blocks.md: The best answer **weighs several factors together**: severity, exploitability, reproducibility as a **success rate**, business impact, reach and detection. A high success rate on a trivial harm ranks below a lower rate on data exfiltration or unauthorised actions. **Validate and deduplicate first**, and **close only after a retest**.

q.q: Automated testing produces 140 variants of the same indirect injection, all exploiting one missing control. How should triage record them?
o: As 140 separate findings, each with its own owner and its own priority rating
As one finding with one root cause, with the variants kept as supporting evidence
As one low-priority finding, because large numbers of variants exaggerate risk
As no finding at all, because automated tools often produce duplicate results
q.why: Variants that share a root cause are one finding, fixed by one control. Keeping the variants as evidence helps the fix and the retest.

scenes.title: Bug, limitation, or both?
scenes.sub: Separating security vulnerabilities from model limitations
scenes.say: Not every bad output is a security vulnerability. A model that confidently invents a fact has a limitation. A system that lets an outsider steal data through the model has a vulnerability. Mix them up, and findings go to the wrong people with the wrong urgency. | This video covers how to tell security vulnerabilities apart from model limitations such as hallucinations, and what to do with each.

scenes.title: Vulnerability or limitation?
rows: A flaw that breaks a security boundary
An inherent weakness in model behaviour
Reduce, ground or warn; rarely eliminate
scenes.say: Four questions separate the two. | Cause: a vulnerability is a flaw that breaks a security boundary, such as access to data or actions. A limitation is an inherent weakness in how the model behaves, such as hallucination or inconsistency. | Adversary: a vulnerability can be exploited on purpose. A limitation often appears in normal use, with no attacker involved. | Fix: a vulnerability can usually be patched, controlled or designed out. A limitation can be reduced, grounded or warned about, but rarely eliminated. | Owner: vulnerabilities go to security vulnerability management, with its deadlines. Limitations go to the model owner’s quality backlog, unless they create a security impact.

scenes.title: Where the line blurs

items.d: Security issues when they unlock real harm
A privacy vulnerability, not just quality
A responsible AI issue with legal stakes
A limitation for the quality backlog

scenes.say: In practice, the line often blurs. | Hallucinated package names are a model limitation, but attackers register those names and wait, so the limitation becomes a supply chain risk. | Jailbreaks bypass safety training. They become security issues when they unlock real harm, such as access to data or dangerous capabilities. | Indirect injection that drives tools is a vulnerability: data has been turned into commands across a trust boundary. | Memorised personal data appearing in outputs is a privacy vulnerability, not just a quality problem. | Biased decisions are a responsible AI issue, with legal stakes in areas like hiring and credit. | And a wrong but harmless answer is a limitation, for the model quality backlog.

scenes.title: Routing a finding
scenes.say: A simple routing question settles most cases. Start with the validated finding. | Ask: does it cross a security boundary, giving access to data, actions or systems that should be protected? | If yes, it is a security vulnerability, managed with security deadlines, whatever role the model plays. | If not, ask whether it causes harm, bias or a policy breach. | If yes, route it to safety and responsible AI review. | If neither, it is a quality limitation, for the model owner’s backlog. Record the reasoning either way, because a finding can change route as the system gains new tools or data.

items: Vulnerabilities break security boundaries; limitations are inherent behaviour
A limitation becomes a vulnerability when it creates security impact
Route each finding to the right owner and process
Record the reasoning, and revisit it when the system changes
scenes.say: To recap. | Vulnerabilities break security boundaries; limitations are inherent model behaviour. | A limitation becomes a vulnerability when it creates security impact. | Route each finding to the right owner and process. | And record the reasoning, revisiting it whenever the system gains new tools or data.

blocks.md:
### Three kinds of finding
- A **security vulnerability** is a weakness an adversary can exploit to compromise **confidentiality, integrity or availability**, or to gain access, data or actions they shouldn’t have. In AI systems, most sit in the **system around the model**: how inputs are trusted, what tools and data the model can reach, and how outputs are handled.
- A **model limitation** is an inherent weakness in model behaviour, such as **hallucination**, inconsistency, sensitivity to phrasing, knowledge gaps or poor calibration (Module 1.3). Limitations appear in normal use, and can be reduced but rarely eliminated.
- **Safety and responsible AI issues**, such as harmful content, bias or unfairness, have their own reviews and, often, legal stakes (Domain 2).

### Classifying common findings
| Finding | Usually | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Hallucinated facts in a summary | Limitation | No adversary and no boundary crossed; reduce with grounding and review |
| Hallucinated package or URL names | Limitation with **security impact** | Attackers can register the names (Module 3.7) |
| A direct jailbreak producing rude content | Safety issue | Bypasses safety training; no security boundary crossed |
| A jailbreak unlocking dangerous capabilities or data | **Vulnerability** | Real harm, deliberately exploitable |
| Indirect injection that triggers tools or leaks data | **Vulnerability** | Untrusted data treated as commands across a trust boundary. **EchoLeak** (CVE-2025-32711, 2025), a zero-click data leak in Microsoft 365 Copilot, is an example |
| Training or personal data appearing in outputs | **Privacy vulnerability** | Disclosure of protected data |
| Biased decisions in hiring or credit | Responsible AI issue | Discrimination law and high-risk obligations apply |

### Why the distinction matters
- **Owners and urgency:** vulnerabilities follow security deadlines; limitations go to the model owner’s backlog.
- **Fixes:** vulnerabilities usually need system controls, such as isolating untrusted content, limiting tools or validating output, rather than only model changes (Module 6.6).
- **Disclosure:** vendor programmes often draw the same line. Google’s AI Vulnerability Reward Program (October 2025), for example, rewards rogue actions and data exfiltration, but treats jailbreaks, direct prompt injection and content issues as out of scope, to be reported through in-product feedback.
- **Honest reporting:** calling every hallucination a vulnerability inflates risk; calling an exploitable injection "model behaviour" hides it.

blocks.title: Vulnerability, limitation or safety issue?
pairs: A summary that invents a meeting date, with no attacker involved
An email that makes the agent forward a customer file to an outsider
A role-play prompt that makes the chatbot swear at users
A coding assistant that keeps recommending a package that doesn’t exist
Another customer’s address appearing in a response

blocks.title: Classification questions
blocks.md: Ask whether the finding **crosses a security boundary** (data, actions, systems). If it does, it is a **vulnerability**, whatever the model’s role. Hallucination alone is a **limitation**, but it becomes a security issue when attackers can exploit it, as with invented package names. Route **safety and fairness** issues to their own reviews.

q.q: A tester shows that an assistant sometimes states incorrect store opening hours. No attacker is involved and no data is exposed. How should this finding be classified?
o: As a critical security vulnerability, requiring an emergency patch within 24 hours
As a model limitation, for the model owner’s quality backlog
As a privacy breach, which must be reported to the regulator
As out of scope, because incorrect outputs are never worth recording
q.why: Incorrect but harmless answers in normal use are a model limitation. Record them for the model owner, with grounding improvements, but don’t treat them as security incidents.

scenes.title: Speaking a common language
scenes.sub: Mapping findings to MITRE ATLAS, OWASP and CWE
scenes.say: A finding described only in your own words is hard to compare, track or share. Mapped to an industry framework, it joins a common language: other teams, vendors and auditors know exactly what kind of problem it is. | This video covers how to correlate assessment findings with industry frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

scenes.title: Frameworks for mapping findings
scenes.say: Six frameworks cover most mapping needs. | MITRE ATLAS describes adversary tactics and techniques against AI, tying each finding to how attackers actually operate. | The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications groups risks into categories, from prompt injection to unbounded consumption. | The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications does the same for agents, from goal hijacking to rogue agents. | CWE names the underlying weakness, such as improper neutralisation of input used for language model prompting. | NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy gives consistent terms for attacks on models. | And CVE identifies specific vulnerabilities in products, while the AI Vulnerability Database collects reports of AI failures.

The ATLAS technique and its sub-technique.

scenes.say: Here is one finding, mapped to several frameworks, because each answers a different question. | MITRE ATLAS says how the attacker operated: the indirect form of its LLM prompt injection technique. | The OWASP lists give the risk categories: prompt injection and excessive agency for LLM applications, and agent goal hijack for agentic applications. | CWE names the underlying weakness: input used for language model prompting that wasn’t neutralised. | And the mapping points to the control gap, email text reaching tool calls, and to a coverage gap: tool misuse cases that haven’t been tested yet.

But one finding often maps to several entries, so record them all. | It shows which categories went untested. But a list of categories isn’t a test plan for your system. | It links findings to real attacker activity, through ATLAS case studies. But a category says nothing about how severe the finding is in your context. | And it supports audits and compliance evidence. But the lists change, so record which version you mapped against.

scenes.say: To recap. | Map findings to MITRE ATLAS, the OWASP lists, CWE and CVE, as relevant. | Each framework answers a different question: how attackers operate, what kind of risk, which weakness, which product flaw. | Use the mappings for coverage analysis, threat intelligence and control selection. | And keep mapping separate from severity, recording the framework versions you used.

blocks.md:
### Frameworks for mapping findings
| Framework | What it classifies | Example mapping |
|---|---|---|
| **MITRE ATLAS** | Adversary tactics, techniques and case studies for AI systems | Indirect prompt injection: AML.T0051.001; LLM jailbreak: AML.T0054; LLM data leakage: AML.T0057 |
| **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)** | LLM01 prompt injection; LLM02 sensitive information disclosure; LLM03 supply chain; LLM04 data and model poisoning; LLM05 improper output handling; LLM06 excessive agency; LLM07 system prompt leakage; LLM08 vector and embedding weaknesses; LLM09 misinformation; LLM10 unbounded consumption | A refund triggered by injected email text: LLM01 and LLM06 |
| **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications** | Agent risks ASI01 to ASI10, such as goal hijack and tool misuse (Module 6.1) | The same finding: ASI01, agent goal hijack |
| **CWE** | Weakness types, including **CWE-1427** (improper neutralisation of input used for LLM prompting) and **CWE-1426** (improper validation of generative AI output) | The injection’s root cause: CWE-1427 |
| **NIST AI 100-2** | Terminology and taxonomy of adversarial ML attacks and mitigations | Classes such as evasion, poisoning and privacy attacks |
| **CVE and AVID** | Specific vulnerabilities in products (CVE); reports of AI failures (AVID) | EchoLeak: CVE-2025-32711 |

### Why correlation matters
- **Common language** with developers, vendors, auditors and regulators.
- **Coverage analysis:** mapping every finding shows which categories were tested and which weren’t, which guides the next assessment (Module 6.4).
- **Threat intelligence:** ATLAS techniques and case studies link findings to real attacker activity, informing priority (Module 6.1).
- **Control mapping:** framework entries point to known mitigations, and to control sets such as ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF (Module 6.6).
- **Trends:** consistent mapping lets you compare assessments over time and across systems.

### Mapping well
- Map **each finding to every relevant entry**: one finding often fits a technique, a risk category and a weakness.
- **Record framework versions**, because the lists are revised; the OWASP LLM list changed substantially for 2025.
- Keep mapping **separate from severity**: a category says what kind of problem it is, not how bad it is in your system.
- Use mappings in **dashboards and reports** to show leadership coverage and recurring weaknesses, not just counts.

blocks.title: Framework mapping questions
blocks.md: Know what each framework is for: **ATLAS** for adversary techniques, **OWASP LLM and Agentic Top 10s** for risk categories, **CWE** for weaknesses, **CVE** for specific product flaws. The best answers **map findings to all relevant entries**, use mappings for **coverage and controls**, and never treat a category as a severity score.

q.q: A team maps every finding from an assessment to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and notices that no findings fall under LLM08 (vector and embedding weaknesses). What is the MOST useful conclusion?
o: The system has no vector or embedding weaknesses, so no further action is needed
The assessment may not have tested the RAG components, so check its coverage
LLM08 has been removed from the latest version of the OWASP list entirely
The team should reclassify some other findings as LLM08 to balance the report
q.why: An empty category is a prompt to check coverage: it may reflect an untested area rather than an absence of weaknesses. Reclassifying findings would distort the report.

blocks.title: If it can’t be reproduced, it can’t be fixed

scenes.title: If it can’t be reproduced, it can’t be fixed
scenes.say: A finding that can’t be reproduced is easy to dispute, hard to fix and impossible to retest. With AI, reproducibility takes extra care, because outputs vary and versions change underneath you. | This video covers how to document evidence and reproducibility steps for AI findings.

scenes.title: What to capture
scenes.say: Capture six kinds of evidence for every AI finding. | Versions: the exact model, system prompt, guardrail configuration and tool definitions in use. | Settings: temperature, random seed where the platform supports one, and other generation parameters. | The full transcript: every turn, input and output, not just the final response. | Traces: what was retrieved, which tools were called, and what actions resulted. | Rates: how many attempts succeeded, out of how many tried. | And integrity: hashes and timestamps for evidence files, with a record of who handled them.

scenes.title: A reproduction package
scenes.code:
environment: staging, release 2026.11.2
model: support-llm 3.4; prompt: system v27
guardrails: policy v9; tools: crm, refund
settings: temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9
input: test email E-12 (stored, not pasted)
expected: summary only, no tool calls
observed: refund tool called, amount 40
rate: 31 of 100 runs, 2-4 Nov 2026
evidence: traces.jsonl sha256 9be1...

notes.d: Everything needed, in one place.
Environment and exact versions.
Settings, and the stored input.
What should happen, and what did.
A rate, not an anecdote.
A hash ends disputes about what traces showed.

scenes.say: Here is a reproduction package for finding F-07. Anyone with access should be able to repeat the test from it. | It records the environment and the exact versions: the release, model, system prompt, guardrail policy and tools. | It records the settings and the input. The test email is stored in the evidence folder, and the package refers to it by name rather than pasting the attack text. | It states what should have happened, a summary with no tool calls, and what actually happened: a refund. | It gives the success rate, thirty-one of a hundred runs, and when the runs took place. | And it fixes the evidence with a hash, so nobody can later dispute what the traces showed.

scenes.title: Handling sensitive evidence

items.d: Refer to attack files by name
Until closure, plus a set period

scenes.say: AI evidence is often sensitive. It can contain personal data, working attack text and harmful outputs, so handle it carefully. | Redact personal data that testers didn’t need to see. | Use placeholders in reports, referring to attack files by name, so a report forwarded by email doesn’t become an attack kit. | Keep raw evidence in restricted storage, with need-to-know access that is logged. | Set retention limits: keep evidence until the finding is closed, plus an agreed period. | Keep a chain of custody: hash evidence when it is captured, and log every hand-off, as Module 5.5 described. | And prepare sanitised packs for sharing with vendors through coordinated disclosure.

scenes.say: To recap. | Capture versions, settings, full transcripts, traces, success rates and integrity data. | Package each finding so anyone with access can reproduce it. | Report rates, pin versions, and reset state between runs. | And protect sensitive evidence, never pasting working attack text into reports.

blocks.md:
### Evidence checklist for AI findings
| Element | What to record |
|---|---|
| **Identification** | Finding ID, title, tester, dates, assessment reference |
| **Environment** | Environment name, release and region; the model, system prompt, guardrail, retrieval index and tool versions (the release manifest, Module 6.2) |
| **Settings** | Temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, seed (where the platform supports it), conversation state |
| **Steps** | Numbered steps from a clean start, referring to stored test inputs by name |
| **Expected and observed** | What should have happened, and what did |
| **Rate** | Successes out of attempts, over what period and with what settings |
| **Traces and artefacts** | Full transcripts, retrieved chunks, tool calls and parameters, logs, screenshots |
| **Impact** | What the result enables, in business terms |
| **Integrity** | Hashes and timestamps of evidence files; chain of custody (Module 5.5) |

### Reproducibility despite non-determinism
- **Report rates, not anecdotes:** "31 of 100 runs" is reproducible in a way that one screenshot isn’t.
- **Pin what you can:** fixed versions, settings and seeds. Hosted models may still vary between runs, and providers update models, so record the provider’s model version or snapshot identifier.
- **Reset state** between runs: memory, caches and planted index content can change results.
- **Keep a minimal case:** the shortest input and fewest steps that still reproduce the finding, which makes fixing and retesting faster.
- **Automate reruns:** store the case in the test harness, so the retest after a fix uses identical conditions (Module 6.6).

### Handling sensitive evidence
- **Redact** personal data that wasn’t needed, and **don’t paste working attack text into reports**: refer to stored files by name, so a forwarded report isn’t an attack kit.
- **Restrict and log access** to raw evidence, and set **retention** to closure plus an agreed period.
- **Prepare sanitised packs** for vendors and coordinated disclosure (Section 5).

blocks.title: The finding nobody could reproduce
blocks.md: A red teamer reports that an HR assistant revealed another employee’s salary. The report contains one screenshot, with no model or prompt versions and no settings. Two weeks later, engineers can’t reproduce the finding, and the provider has updated the model in the meantime.

q.q: What would MOST have prevented this dispute?
o: A higher-resolution screenshot, showing the full conversation window clearly
A reproduction package: versions, settings, transcript, traces and success rate
A verbal briefing for the engineering team, given on the day of the test
A rule that only findings engineers can reproduce are recorded at all
q.why: Versions, settings, full transcripts, traces and a success rate let engineers reproduce the conditions, or show that the model change affected the result. Screenshots and verbal briefings lack that detail, and refusing to record unreproduced findings hides risk.

blocks.title: Evidence questions
blocks.md: Strong answers produce a **reproduction package**: exact **versions** (model, prompt, guardrails, tools), **settings**, the **full transcript and traces**, **expected versus observed** results, a **success rate**, and **hashed** evidence with a chain of custody. Sensitive evidence is **redacted and restricted**, and reports refer to attack inputs **by name**.

q.q: Why should reports refer to stored attack inputs by name rather than pasting the full attack text?
o: Attack text is usually too long to fit into the report’s page layout
Reports get forwarded, and pasted attack text could be reused by others
Regulators require attack inputs to be stored in one specific file format
Named references make the report look more professional to executives
q.why: Reports circulate widely. Keeping attack text in restricted evidence storage, referenced by name, stops a forwarded report from becoming a ready-made attack kit.

scenes.title: Same finding, different audiences
scenes.sub: Communicating AI risk to technical and non-technical stakeholders
scenes.say: The same finding needs telling differently to an engineer, a product owner, a lawyer and a board. Get it wrong, and engineers lack the detail to fix it, while executives either panic or shrug. | This video covers risk communication strategies for technical and non-technical stakeholders.

scenes.title: What each audience needs
rows: Root cause, repro steps, fix options
scenes.say: Each audience needs something different. | Engineers want the root cause, reproduction steps and fix options. Leaders want the business impact, the decisions needed, and the cost of acting or not acting. Legal and risk teams want obligations, exposure and deadlines. | Engineers work from tickets, traces and test cases. Leaders need a one-page summary and trends. Legal and risk teams need register entries and memos. | And the language changes: technical and precise for engineers; plain and quantified for leaders; and exact about facts and duties for legal teams.

scenes.code:

notes.d: The same finding, told for leaders.
The decision and its cost, first.
Honest numbers, real consequences.
A decision, a deadline.
Say what isn’t urgent.

scenes.say: Here is an executive summary of the same refund finding, on one page, in plain words. | It starts with the bottom line: delay the launch by a week to fix two problems. | It states the risk in business terms, with honest numbers: customers can trigger unapproved refunds, it worked in thirty-one of a hundred attempts, and the impact is direct loss and possible regulatory interest. | It offers options, fixing first or launching without the refund tool, and makes a clear request with a deadline. | And it keeps proportion, saying what isn’t urgent, so the serious finding stands out without alarm.

scenes.title: Principles for AI risk communication

items.d: A calm tone and consistent ratings

scenes.say: Six principles make AI risk communication work. | Bottom line first: lead with the decision needed, and the impact. | Quantify honestly: success rates, ranges and uncertainty, rather than "it can be hacked". | Speak business: loss, customers, legal exposure and reputation. | No hype and no dismissal: keep a calm tone, and use the same rating scale every time. | Offer options: fix, mitigate, accept or avoid, each with its cost and residual risk. | And show, don’t shock: describe harmful outputs, or show redacted examples, rather than pasting them into slides.

items: Tailor content and format to each audience
Lead with the bottom line, in business terms
Quantify honestly; state what testing can’t show
Offer options; disclose third-party flaws responsibly
scenes.say: To recap. | Tailor the content and the format to each audience. | Lead with the bottom line, in business terms. | Quantify honestly, and say what testing can’t show. | And offer options, disclosing flaws in third-party products responsibly, through the vendor’s programme.

blocks.md:
### Tailoring the message
| Audience | Needs | Format |
|---|---|---|
| **Engineers and model owners** | Root cause, reproduction package, affected components, fix options, retest criteria | Tickets with evidence links; test cases in the harness |
| **Security leadership** | Severity, trends, framework mapping, coverage, detection gaps | Findings register; dashboards |
| **Executives and the board** | Business impact, decisions needed, options with cost and residual risk, position against risk appetite | One-page summary; trend charts; risk register extracts |
| **Legal, privacy and compliance** | Personal data involved, regulatory duties (such as GDPR breach notification or AI Act serious incident reporting), disclosure decisions | Memo with facts, timeline and options |
| **Product owners** | User impact, launch implications, workarounds | Briefing with options and timelines |
| **Vendors** | A reproducible, sanitised report of a flaw in their product | Coordinated disclosure through their programme |

### Structuring an assessment report
1. **Executive summary:** the bottom line, top risks in business terms, and the decisions needed.
2. **Scope and method:** what was tested, how and when, and what was out of scope, so readers know the limits of the conclusions.
3. **Findings:** each with its rating, evidence, framework mapping and recommendation.
4. **Positive observations:** controls that held, which helps decision-makers and teams.
5. **Recommendations and roadmap:** prioritised fixes, owners and retest plans.
6. **Appendices:** reproduction packages and the coverage matrix, with restricted access.

### Communicating uncertainty and residual risk
- Use **rates and confidence**, such as "31 of 100 attempts" or "below 1% in 2,000 attempts", not "rarely".
- State what testing **can’t show**: passing tests reduce uncertainty, but don’t prove the absence of vulnerabilities.
- Describe the **residual risk** after fixes, and who has accepted it (Module 6.6).

### Coordinated disclosure
Report flaws in third-party products to the vendor privately, through its vulnerability disclosure or bug bounty programme, with reasonable time to fix before anything is published. **ISO/IEC 29147** covers vulnerability disclosure, and **ISO/IEC 30111** covers vendors’ vulnerability handling. Check the vendor’s scope first, because some programmes handle content issues separately from security flaws (Section 2).

blocks.title: The board slide
blocks.md: A security lead plans to show the board a slide listing all 47 findings from a red team exercise, each with a severity score and a MITRE ATLAS technique ID, plus a screenshot of the most offensive output the red team produced.

q.q: What is the BEST improvement to the board presentation?
o: Add full reproduction steps for each finding, so board members can verify them
Lead with business impact and the decisions needed, with trends and no raw outputs
Remove every finding rated below critical, so the board only sees the worst five
Replace the screenshot with an even more shocking example, to help secure budget
q.why: Boards need business impact, decisions and trends, in plain language. Technical detail belongs in appendices and tickets, hiding lower findings misleads, and shocking content distracts and may cause harm.

blocks.title: Risk communication questions
blocks.md: Match the message to the **audience**: technical detail for engineers; **business impact, options and decisions** for leaders; **obligations and facts** for legal teams. Lead with the **bottom line**, **quantify honestly**, avoid both **hype and dismissal**, and disclose third-party flaws through **coordinated disclosure**.

q.q: Which statement BEST communicates a red team result to executives?
o: "The model is fundamentally insecure, and anyone could hack it at any moment"
"Customers triggered unapproved refunds in 31% of tests; we advise a week’s delay"
"We found an AML.T0051.001 issue mapping to LLM01 and LLM06, with a high score"
"Testing found a few problems, but AI always has issues, so no action is needed"
q.why: It states the business impact with an honest number and a clear recommendation. The others are alarmist, too technical for the audience, or dismissive.

quiz.q: Why is reproducibility reported as a success rate for AI findings?
o: Success rates are mandatory under every AI security regulation in force
AI outputs vary, so the rate shows how often the attack actually works
A rate is easier to calculate than recording the result of a single test
Rates hide the details of the attack from anyone who reads the report
quiz.why: Because outputs vary between attempts, a rate over many runs, with settings recorded, is the meaningful measure of reproducibility.

quiz.q: Why should findings be deduplicated during triage?
o: Duplicates make reports longer than executives are willing to read
Variants with one root cause need one fix, so they are one finding
Deduplication lowers the severity of each finding that remains afterwards
Most frameworks only allow one finding per assessment to be reported
quiz.why: Grouping variants under one root cause gives one owner, one fix and one retest, with the variants kept as evidence.

quiz.q: Why does a finding that went undetected during testing deserve a higher priority?
o: Undetected findings are always easier to fix than detected ones
An attacker could exploit it without anyone noticing or responding
Detection tools are only required for high-risk AI systems by law
Monitoring teams are responsible for fixing every undetected finding
quiz.why: Without detection, exploitation could continue unnoticed, so the exposure lasts longer and response is delayed.

quiz.q: What makes a finding a security vulnerability rather than a model limitation?
o: It appears in more than half of all the test attempts that were made
It lets someone cross a security boundary, reaching data, actions or systems
It was found by the security team rather than by the data science team
It involves a model that was provided by an external third-party vendor
quiz.why: Vulnerabilities break security boundaries and can be exploited deliberately; limitations are inherent behaviour seen in normal use.

quiz.q: When does a hallucination become a security concern?
o: Whenever the model is used by more than a thousand people each day
When attackers can exploit it, as with invented package names
Only when the hallucination appears in an image rather than text
Never, because hallucinations are only quality problems
quiz.why: Hallucination is a limitation, but invented package or URL names can be registered by attackers, creating supply chain risk.

quiz.q: Where should a finding about biased outputs in a hiring tool usually be routed?
o: To the network team, as a firewall configuration problem
To safety and responsible AI review, given its legal stakes
To the help desk, as a routine user complaint about tone
To nobody, since bias is not a security issue of any kind
quiz.why: Bias is a responsible AI issue with legal implications, such as discrimination law and high-risk obligations, so it needs its own review.

quiz.q: What does MITRE ATLAS add when mapping a finding?
o: A severity score that replaces the organisation’s own risk rating
The adversary technique involved, linked to tactics and case studies
A legal opinion on whether the finding must be reported to regulators
A ready-made patch for the vulnerability, supplied by MITRE itself
quiz.why: ATLAS describes how adversaries attack AI systems, with tactics, techniques and real case studies.

quiz.q: Which CWE entry describes improper neutralisation of input used for LLM prompting?
o: CWE-79, which covers cross-site scripting in web pages
CWE-1427, which covers input used for LLM prompting
CWE-89, which covers SQL injection into databases
CWE-200, which covers exposure of sensitive information
quiz.why: CWE-1427 names the weakness behind prompt injection; CWE-1426 covers improper validation of generative AI output.

quiz.q: What should a reproduction package for an AI finding include?
o: A single screenshot of the most convincing output, with no other detail at all
Versions, settings, transcript, traces, expected and observed results, and a rate
The tester’s opinion of how serious the finding is, with no supporting data
The full text of every attack prompt, pasted into the report’s executive summary
quiz.why: Those elements let anyone repeat the test under the same conditions and verify the fix later.

quiz.q: Why should evidence files be hashed when they are captured?
o: Hashing compresses evidence so it takes less storage space
It proves later that the evidence hasn’t been altered
Hashes make evidence readable by automated report tools
Regulators only accept evidence stored in hashed form
quiz.why: A hash recorded at capture, with a chain of custody, lets anyone confirm the evidence is unchanged.

quiz.q: What does "bottom line up front" mean in an executive summary?
o: Listing every finding in order of when it was discovered
Leading with the decision that is needed, and its impact
Placing the budget request on the final page of the report
Starting with the technical method used by the testers
quiz.why: Leaders need the decision and its consequences first; supporting detail follows.

quiz.q: How should a flaw found in a third-party AI product be disclosed?
o: Published immediately on social media, to warn the vendor’s other customers
Reported privately to the vendor, with time to fix before any publication
Kept secret indefinitely, since disclosure could embarrass the vendor
Sent to all the vendor’s competitors, so that they can check their products
quiz.why: Coordinated vulnerability disclosure, as described in ISO/IEC 29147, protects users while giving the vendor time to fix.

quiz.q: Why should an assessment report include positive observations?
o: To make the testing team look good to the people who hired them
To show which controls held, which helps decisions and teams
To reduce the number of findings that need to be fixed later
To satisfy a legal requirement in every country for reports
quiz.why: Knowing what worked helps leaders judge overall risk, and tells teams which controls to keep and extend.

exam.q: A red team reports a jailbreak that makes a public chatbot produce mildly offensive jokes in 45% of attempts, and an indirect injection that leaks other customers’ order details in 2% of attempts. Which should receive the HIGHER priority?
o: The jailbreak, because its 45% success rate makes it far more reproducible
The injection, because leaking customers’ data is far more severe at scale
Both equally, because every finding should always share the same priority
Neither, because both success rates fall below the 50% threshold for action
exam.why: Severity and business impact dominate: a data leak affecting customers is serious, and 2% is frequent at scale. The jailbreak still needs fixing, at lower priority.

exam.q: During triage, an engineer argues that a finding should be closed because the fix "has been deployed". The retest hasn’t been run. What should happen?
o: Close it, since the engineer has confirmed that the fix was deployed
Keep it open until a retest under the original conditions passes
Lower its priority to P3, since a fix now exists in production
Delete the finding, so it doesn’t appear in the next report
exam.why: Closure requires evidence: a retest using the reproduction package confirms the fix works and hasn’t been bypassed.

exam.q: An assistant sometimes recommends a software library that doesn’t exist. Researchers note that attackers have started registering such names. How should this finding be treated?
o: As a harmless hallucination, for the model’s quality backlog only
As a limitation with security impact, needing supply chain controls
As a direct jailbreak, to be handled through content moderation alone
As out of scope, since the library names were never real
exam.why: The hallucination is a limitation, but because attackers can register the names, it creates supply chain risk that needs controls such as allow-listed registries.

exam.q: A vendor’s AI bug bounty programme lists jailbreaks and direct prompt injection as out of scope, but rewards data exfiltration. A tester finds that a planted document makes the vendor’s assistant send users’ files to an outside address. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Don’t report it at all, since prompt injection is listed as out of scope
Report it through the programme as data exfiltration, a security impact
Publish the finding at once, since the programme won’t accept it anyway
Report it only through in-product feedback, as a content issue
exam.why: Indirect injection that exfiltrates data has a security impact, which is exactly what such programmes reward. The exclusions cover content-only issues.

exam.q: A team maps its findings only to internal labels such as "chatbot weirdness" and "agent problem". What is the MAIN drawback?
o: Internal labels can’t be stored in standard ticketing systems at all
Findings can’t be compared, shared or checked for coverage consistently
Internal labels always overstate severity compared with frameworks
The team must pay a licence fee to use internal labels in reports
exam.why: Mapping to ATLAS, OWASP and CWE gives a common language, supports coverage analysis and links findings to known controls and threats.

exam.q: A dashboard shows findings mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, and an executive concludes that LLM01 findings are always the most severe. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, since the OWASP list is ordered by severity in every system
Explain that categories describe the type of risk, not its severity here
Remove LLM01 findings from the dashboard to avoid further confusion
Re-rate every LLM01 finding as critical, to match the executive’s view
exam.why: Framework categories classify the kind of problem. Severity depends on context, so mapping and rating must stay separate.

exam.q: Engineers can’t reproduce a finding that the red team recorded a month ago. The record shows the provider has since updated the model behind the API. What does this MOST suggest about evidence practice?
o: Findings from hosted models should never be recorded in the first place
Record the provider’s model version or snapshot, and retest after changes
The red team must have invented the finding, so it should be closed
Engineers should be given administrator access to the provider’s systems
exam.why: Recording the exact provider model version explains changed results, and retesting after provider updates checks whether the risk remains.

exam.q: A red team’s report pastes full attack transcripts, including working injection text and customer names, into the main body. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Encrypt the PDF with a strong password, and keep the content exactly as it is
Redact personal data, store attack text separately, and refer to it by name
Delete all of the evidence immediately, so that nobody can ever misuse it
Email the report only to the executives, and not to any of the engineers
exam.why: Reports circulate. Redaction and restricted evidence storage, referenced by name, protect people and stop the report from becoming an attack kit, while engineers can still reproduce the finding.

exam.q: A CISO must brief the board on an AI red team exercise with two serious findings and many minor ones. Which approach is BEST?
o: Present every finding in technical detail, so the board sees how thorough the work was
Lead with the two risks in business terms, the decisions needed and the options
Mention only the minor findings, to avoid alarming the board unnecessarily
Present the most shocking raw outputs, to make sure the board takes AI seriously
exam.why: Boards need the bottom line: business impact, decisions and options, with proportion. Detail, minimisation and shock tactics all undermine good decisions.

exam.q: A product owner asks whether the absence of findings in one category means the assistant is safe in that area. What is the MOST accurate answer?
o: Yes: no findings means the category has now been proven to be completely safe
Testing reduces uncertainty, but can’t prove absence; check coverage and limits
No: categories with no findings are always the most dangerous ones in practice
It depends only on how much the testing cost, not on what was tested
exam.why: Honest communication states what testing can and can’t show: coverage, attempts and conditions determine how much confidence is justified.
